<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>Key Findings</h3>

<div id="A7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We highlight our key findings, which may facilitate the community in better reproducing our work.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The importance of base checkpoint: </span> During the initial phase of our development, we experimented with smaller-scale models, specifically a 7B dense model and a 16B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, as the foundational architectures for RL training. However, these configurations consistently failed to yield meaningful improvements when evaluated on the AIME benchmark, which we employed as the primary validation set. We observed that as response lengths increased, these smaller models exhibited a tendency toward repetition and were unable to effectively leverage long chains of thought (CoT) to improve reasoning accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address these limitations, we transitioned to larger-scale models, including a 32B dense model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen, 2024a</a>)</cite>, a 230B MoE model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2024a</a>)</cite>, and a 671B MoE model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2024b</a>)</cite>. With these more capable architectures, we finally observed substantial performance gains attributable to pure RL training. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of reinforcement learning from base models is highly dependent on the underlying model capacity. We therefore recommend that future research in this area prioritize the use of sufficiently large and expressive models when aiming to validate the efficacy of RL from scratch.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The importance of verifiers: </span>The effectiveness of DeepSeek-R1-Zero is highly contingent upon the reliability and fidelity of the reward signal used during training. To date, our investigations indicate that two approaches—rule-based reward models (RMs) and LLMs to assess an answer’s correctness against a predefined ground-truth—serve as robust mechanisms for mitigating issues related to reward hacking. The LLM-based evaluation framework demonstrates particular effectiveness for tasks with well-defined, concise answers, such as single-sentence or phrase-level responses. However, this method exhibits limited generalizability to more complex tasks, including open-ended generation and long-form writing, where the notion of correctness is inherently more subjective and nuanced.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Iterative pipeline:</span> We propose a multi-stage training pipeline comprising both SFT and RL stages. The RL component enables the model to explore and discover optimal reasoning trajectories for tasks capabilities that cannot be fully realized through human-annotated reasoning traces alone. In particular, without the RL stage, long-chain reasoning patterns, such as those required in complex Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, would remain largely unexplored. Conversely, the SFT stage plays a crucial role in tasks where reliable reward signals are difficult to define or model, such as open-ended question answering and creative writing. Therefore, both RL and SFT are indispensable components of our training pipeline. Exclusive reliance on RL can lead to reward hacking and suboptimal behavior in ill-posed tasks, while depending solely on SFT may prevent the model from optimizing its reasoning capabilities through exploration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Unsuccessful Attempts</h3>

<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the early stages of developing DeepSeek-R1, we also encountered failures and setbacks along the way. We share our failure experiences here to provide insights, but this does not imply that these approaches are incapable of developing effective reasoning models.</p>
</div>
<section id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Process Reward Model (PRM)</h5>

<div id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PRM is a reasonable method to guide the model toward better approaches for solving reasoning tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Uesato et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>. However, in practice, PRM has three main limitations that may hinder its ultimate success. First, it is challenging to explicitly define a fine-grain step in general reasoning.
Second, determining whether the current intermediate step is correct is a challenging task. Automated annotation using models may not yield satisfactory results, while manual annotation is not conducive to scaling up.
Third, once a model-based PRM is introduced, it inevitably leads to reward hacking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and retraining the reward model needs additional training resources and it complicates the whole training pipeline. In conclusion, while PRM demonstrates a good ability to rerank the top-N responses generated by the model or assist in guided search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Snell et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, its advantages are limited compared to the additional computational overhead it introduces during the large-scale reinforcement learning process in our experiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)</h5>

<div id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Inspired by AlphaGo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silver et al., 2017b</a>)</cite> and AlphaZero <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silver et al., 2017a</a>)</cite>, we explored using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to enhance test-time compute scalability. This approach involves breaking answers into smaller parts to allow the model to explore the solution space systematically. To facilitate this, we prompt the model to generate multiple tags that correspond to specific reasoning steps necessary for the search. For training, we first use collected prompts to find answers via MCTS guided by a pre-trained value model. Subsequently, we use the resulting question-answer pairs to train both the actor model and the value model, iteratively refining the process.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, this approach encounters several challenges when scaling up the training. First, unlike chess, where the search space is relatively well-defined, token generation presents an exponentially larger search space. To address this, we set a maximum extension limit for each node, but this can lead to the model getting stuck in local optima. Second, the value model directly influences the quality of generation since it guides each step of the search process. Training a fine-grained value model is inherently difficult, which makes it challenging for the model to iteratively improve. While AlphaGo’s core success relied on training a value model to progressively enhance its performance, this principle proves difficult to replicate in our setup due to the complexities of token generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In conclusion, while MCTS can improve performance during inference when paired with a pre-trained value model, iteratively boosting model performance through self-search remains a significant challenge.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="A8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Chain-of-thought Reasoning</h3>

<div id="A8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022b</a>)</cite> revolutionized how LLMs approach complex reasoning tasks by prompting them to generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing a final answer.
This method significantly improved performance on benchmarks involving arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning. Subsequent work explored its scope: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al. (2023)</a></cite> demonstrated that CoT’s effectiveness scales with model size, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kojima et al. (2022)</a></cite> extended it to zero-shot settings by simply instructing models to “think step by step.”</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Building on CoT’s framework, numerous “prompt engineering” techniques have been proposed to enhance model performance.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023b)</a></cite> introduced self-consistency, a method that aggregates answers from multiple reasoning paths to improve robustness and accuracy.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2023a)</a></cite> developed least-to-most prompting, which decomposes complex problems into sequential subquestions that are solved incrementally.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al. (2023a)</a></cite> proposed tree-of-thoughts, enabling models to explore multiple reasoning branches simultaneously and perform deliberate decision-making through looking ahead or backtracking.
Collectively, these approaches leverage human prior knowledge and more structured reasoning frameworks to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.2 </span>Scaling Inference-time Compute</h3>

<div id="A8.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As unsupervised pre-training scaling might be constrained by the amount of available human data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muennighoff et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, scaling compute during inference has become even more critical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Snell et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Broadly, we define methods that improve model performance by increasing inference compute as forms of scaling inference-time compute.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A straightforward approach trades compute for performance by generating multiple diverse reasoning chains and selecting the best answer. The optimal answer can be identified using a separate reranker <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, process-based reward models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Uesato et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or simply by selecting the most common answer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>.
Search methods, such as Monte Carlo Tree Search and Beam Search, also guide exploration of the solution space more effectively <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trinh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Beyond parallel generation, self-correct techniques prompt or train models to iteratively critique and refine their outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Welleck et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, often incorporating external feedback to enhance reliability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
Additionally, some methods improve performance by integrating tool use during testing, which is particularly effective for knowledge-intensive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nakano et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and compute-intensive tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Test-time training (TTT) further updates the model during inference to boost performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Akyürek et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. There are also various other inference-time scaling approaches that—either implicitly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or explicitly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2024</a>)</cite>—allocate more compute for each token.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, our work shows that LLMs can achieve scalable improvements through additional RL compute and increased test-time compute (i.e., more tokens). We integrate the benefits of scaling at test time into a broader framework that uses reinforcement learning to incentivize enhanced in-context search abilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.3 </span>Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Enhancement</h3>

<div id="A8.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement Learning plays a pivotal role in aligning LLMs with human preferences <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Despite its importance, few studies have focused on using RL to enhance reasoning capabilities. Traditional RL pipelines begin with SFT on high-quality human demonstrations, which provides a strong initialization and prevents mode collapse. Following this, a reward model is trained on human preferences, and the language model is subsequently optimized using methods such as PPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017</a>)</cite> or DPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Although this method works well for alignment, it risks constraining models to emulate human reasoning patterns, potentially hindering the discovery of novel problem-solving strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Methods like STaR iteratively boost performance by fine-tuning on the model’s self-generated chain-of-thought that leads to correct final answers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Recent studies have also investigated the use of process-based rewards that emphasize both the correctness of final answers and the soundness of the reasoning processes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Unlike these methods, our work applies outcome-based RL directly to base language models without an initial SFT phase. This design choice encourages the emergence of innovative and unconstrained reasoning strategies, enabling the model to develop diverse solutions beyond mere imitation of human examples.
Our approach also inspired further exploration in subsequent research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Face, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">

<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To promote the development of the open-source community and industry ecosystem, we have made the model weights of <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1</a> and <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Zero" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Zero</a> publicly available on HuggingFace. In addition, we release <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B</a>, <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B</a>, <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B</a>, <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B</a>, <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B</a>, <a href="https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B</a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we have released the fundamental model inference code (<a href="https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3</a>) and provided detailed usage guidelines (<a href="https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1</a>) on GitHub.</p>

<span id="A10.T23.7.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T23.7.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Quantum entanglement is the phenomenon that occurs when a group of particles are generated, interact, or share spatial proximity in such a way that the quantum state of each particle of the group cannot be described independently of the state of the others, including when the particles are separated by a large distance. The topic of quantum entanglement is at the heart of the disparity between classical and quantum physics: entanglement is a primary feature of quantum mechanics not present in classical mechanics.</span></span>
<span id="A10.T23.7.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T23.7.2.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Measurements of physical properties such as position, momentum, spin, and polarization performed on entangled particles can, in some cases, be found to be perfectly correlated. For example, if a pair of entangled particles is generated such that their total spin is known to be zero, and one particle is found to have clockwise spin on a first axis, then the spin of the other particle, measured on the same axis, is found to be anticlockwise. However, this behavior gives rise to seemingly paradoxical effects: any measurement of a particle’s properties results in an apparent and irreversible wave function collapse of that particle and changes the original quantum state. With entangled particles, such measurements affect the entangled system as a whole.</span></span>
<span id="A10.T23.7.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T23.7.2.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Such phenomena were the subject of a 1935 paper by Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky, and Nathan Rosen, and several papers by Erwin Schrödinger shortly thereafter, describing what came to be known as the EPR paradox. Einstein and others considered such behavior impossible, as it violated the local realism view of causality (Einstein referring to it as "spooky action at a distance") and argued that the accepted formulation of quantum mechanics must therefore be incomplete.</span></span>

It focuses on measuring model performance in open-ended tasks, with particular emphasis on coding and mathematics-related prompts.
Given the inherently subjective nature of open-ended tasks, where multiple valid responses may exist, the benchmark necessitates the use of an evaluation model to approximate human judgment effectively. Higher evaluation scores suggest that the model is more likely to be favored by human users in real-world scenarios. </figcaption>

<span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Then consider if the assistant’s answers are helpful, relevant, and concise. Note when user prompt has any ambiguity or more than one interpretation, it is more helpful and appropriate to ask for clarifications or more information from the user than providing an answer based on assumptions. Relevant means all parts of the response closely connect or are appropriate to what is being asked. Concise means the response is clear and not verbose or excessive.</span></span>
<span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Then consider the creativity and novelty of the assistant’s answers when needed. Finally, identify any missing important information in the assistants’ answers that would be beneficial to include when responding to the user prompt.</span></span>
<span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">After providing your explanation, you must output only one of the following choices as your final verdict with a label:</span></span>
<span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1. Assistant A is significantly better: [[A</span><math id="A10.T25.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo><mo lspace="0em">⁣</mo><mo mathsize="0.900em">&gt;</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;&gt;</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T25.4.4.1.1.7.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">B]]</span></span>
</span></td></tr>

For example, </span><math id="A10.T32.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="81" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">81</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">81</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T32.4.2.1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> is </span><math id="A10.T32.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">13</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T32.4.2.1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">-eautiful because </span><math id="A10.T32.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="81=\underline{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">81</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><munder accentunder="true"><mn mathsize="0.900em">6</mn><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">81=\underline{6}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T32.4.2.1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><math id="A10.T32.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{3}_{13}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mn mathsize="0.900em">3</mn><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mn mathsize="0.900em">13</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{3}_{13}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T32.4.2.1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> and </span><math id="A10.T32.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6+3=\sqrt{81}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">6</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">3</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><msqrt><mn mathsize="0.900em">81</mn></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6+3=\sqrt{81}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T32.4.2.1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
